title: Families of Four in a Theater
statement:
A theater has n rows, numbered from 1. Every row has 10 seats, numbered 1 to 10 from left to right. There is an aisle between seats 3 and 4 and another between seats 7 and 8.

Some seats are already sold: reserved[i] = [row, seat]. All pairs are distinct.

A family of four must sit in 4 neighboring seats of one row, and an aisle may only run exactly through the middle of the family. So the only places a family fits are seats 2–5, 4–7 and 6–9. Return the largest number of families you can seat.

examples.why: Row 1: seat 5 blocks 2–5 and 4–7, but 6–9 is free. Row 2: only the wall seats are taken, so both 2–5 and 6–9 fit.
Both side blocks are broken, but the middle block 4–7 is untouched. Checking only the two halves would answer 0.
Every untouched row seats 2 families, and row 7 still seats 1. Looping over a billion rows is too slow.

hints: Only rows with at least one sold seat can hold fewer than 2 families. How many rows is that, at most?
A row seats 2 families only with 2–5 and 6–9 both free. Otherwise it seats 1 if any of 2–5, 4–7, 6–9 is free, else 0.
Group the reservations by row (a map from row to a bitmask of sold seats). Untouched rows give 2 each: 2 · (n − rows in the map).

explain.intuition:
Seats 1 and 10 never matter, and a row can hold at most 2 families (2–5 plus 6–9). The block 4–7 overlaps both of them, so it only helps when both side blocks are broken but the middle is free.

With n up to a billion, you cannot visit every row. But only rows that appear in reserved can lose anything, and there are at most 10 000 of them. Store each such row's sold seats as a bitmask, test the three blocks with a single & each, and give every other row 2 families without looking at it.
steps: Build a map from row to bitmask: for [row, seat], set bit seat.
Start with total = 2 · (n − map.size) for the untouched rows.
For each mask: if blocks 2–5 and 6–9 are both free, add 2.
Otherwise add 1 if any of 2–5, 4–7 or 6–9 is free.
pitfalls: Forgetting the middle block 4–7. Row [3, 8] sold still seats one family.
Counting 2–5 and 4–7 (or 4–7 and 6–9) as two families. They share seats 4 and 5 (or 6 and 7).
Looping over all n rows. It times out when n is a billion.

solutions.title: A set of sold seats per touched row
solutions.idea: Visiting all n rows is too slow, so group the sales by row. For each touched row, check the four seats of each block against that row's set. Every other row seats 2.

solutions.title: Bitmask per touched row
solutions.idea: Only rows with a sale can seat fewer than 2. Keep one bitmask per such row and test each block with a single AND.

followups: Families can now be of any size s and an aisle may split them anywhere. How do you count per row?
Reservations arrive one at a time and you must report the answer after each. What do you update?
